claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a pure Cu matrix.
The starting composite is produced by conventional powder metallurgy and sintering under an inert atmosphere.
The proposed intervention is to add 0.5–1 at.% Zr to the Cu matrix using pre-alloyed powders.
Adding 0.5–1 at.% Zr to the Cu matrix will induce Zr-enriched nanoprecipitates at W–Cu interfaces during sintering.
Zirconium has a strong tendency to segregate at metal interfaces.
The Zr-enriched interfacial nanoprecipitates will act as diffusion barriers at W–Cu interfaces.
The proposed diffusion barrier will limit interdiffusion between W and Cu.
Limiting W–Cu interdiffusion will suppress phase separation.
The Zr-derived interfacial barrier will inhibit the nucleation and growth of interfacial voids during prolonged thermal and irradiation exposure.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo interfacial degradation and void formation under the stated service conditions.
Interfacial degradation and void formation diminish the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
Zr-doped W–Cu composites will retain more stable interfaces and form fewer voids than undoped composites during service.
Zr-doped W–Cu composites will exhibit higher thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu composites under equivalent heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The predicted thermal-conductivity improvement will result from enhanced W–Cu interfacial stability and reduced void formation.
The intervention is applicable to conventionally powder-metallurgically processed W–Cu composites when sintering remains below approximately 1000 °C.
Excessive Zr-containing intermetallic-phase formation could impair thermal transport.
